name: Toby Jug
desc: A jug shaped like a stout man in a tricorn hat, a Staffordshire favourite since the 1700s. Somebody's nan had four.

name: Staffordshire Flatback
desc: A pottery figure with no back, because it was made to stand on a mantelpiece and be admired from the front.

name: Goss Crested China Pot
desc: A tiny white pot with a town crest on it, bought by seaside visitors by the thousand. This one has Macclesfield's.

name: Goss Crested China Jug
desc: A thimble-sized jug with Buxton's crest. Buxton water was the thing, and the souvenir was the next best.

name: Goss Crested China Urn
desc: A small urn with a Conwy crest, from the days when every day-tripper came home with a shelf of these.

name: Bakelite Radio
desc: A brown wireless the size of a bread bin. It still smells faintly of warm dust and the Home Service.

name: Brass Miner's Lamp
desc: A lamp that went down the pit on a hundred shifts and came up again every time.

name: Clarice Cliff Saucer
desc: Bold orange and yellow stripes from the Potteries in the 1930s. The cup went years ago.

name: Wade Whimsie
desc: A tiny glazed animal made in Burslem. They came in boxes of five and everyone wanted the one they hadn't got.

name: Stereoscope Card
desc: Two nearly identical photographs of a Victorian pier. Through the viewer, the pier leaps out at you.

name: Dinky Toy Bus
desc: A die-cast double-decker with most of its paint. Made in Liverpool, played with on the lino.

name: Penny Black (Fake)
desc: The first adhesive stamp, 1840, or a very hopeful copy of one. The perforations are too good, which gives it away.

name: Ration Book
desc: A buff little book of coupons from the war years, with someone's careful signature in the front.

name: 1966 Final Ticket
desc: A stub from the 1966 World Cup final at Wembley. Whether it is real is a matter for the pub to settle.

name: Miniature Tin Bath
desc: A toy-sized zinc bath, a nod to Friday nights in front of the fire before indoor plumbing.

name: Horse Brass
desc: A polished brass disc that once hung from a carthorse's harness, and now from a pub beam.

name: Souvenir Thimble
desc: A silver-coloured thimble with a view of Blackpool Tower. Never used for sewing.

name: Tin Penny-Farthing
desc: A clockwork tin cyclist with a very large front wheel and a very small ambition.

name: Gallopers Horse
desc: A carved wooden horse from a fairground roundabout, with a bright eye and a chipped ear.

name: Cut-glass Decanter
desc: Heavy, sparkly and for best. The sherry in it is older than you are.

name: Silver Pocket Watch
desc: It ticks, loses four minutes a day, and has a dent where someone sat on it in 1952.

name: Cigarette Card Set
desc: Twenty-five little cards of British birds, collected one packet at a time, with a gap where the wren should be.

name: Bell Punch Ticket Machine
desc: A conductor's ticket machine that goes ting. Cheaper than a bus fare and just as noisy.

name: Jubilee Mug
desc: A commemorative mug from a street party, with bunting on one side and a crown on the other.

name: Coronation Biscuit Tin
desc: A tin from 1953. Whatever is in there now is not biscuits, but buttons.

name: Engraved Slate Coaster
desc: A slate coaster with a hill on it. Welsh slate roofed half the country and now it holds your tea.

name: Welsh Lovespoon
desc: A carved wooden spoon, a courting gift in Wales for centuries. Every symbol on the handle means something, and some of it is a hint.

name: Claddagh Ring
desc: Two hands holding a crowned heart, from Galway. Which way round you wear it tells everyone your business.

name: Silver Quaich
desc: A two-handled Scottish drinking cup, passed round for welcome and farewell.

name: Shortbread Tin
desc: A tartan tin with a stag on the lid. It holds sewing things now and has done since 1987.

name: Bog Oak Carving
desc: A Celtic cross carved from wood that lay in an Irish bog for thousands of years. Black as coal and very smooth.

name: Blarney Pebble
desc: A pebble from Cork, sold as a bit of the famous stone. It is a pebble. It is lucky anyway.

name: Tara Brooch Copy
desc: A copy of the great Irish brooch from the 700s, small enough to lose in a coat.

name: Fine Lace Shawl
desc: A shawl so fine that, they say, you can pull it through a wedding ring.

name: Fresnel Prism
desc: A glass prism from a lighthouse lamp. Held to the window, it throws small rainbows at the lino.

name: Colliery Check Tag
desc: A numbered brass tag. Every man took one down the pit and handed it back at the top, so they knew who was out.

name: Mill Bobbin
desc: A wooden bobbin from a Lancashire cotton mill, worn smooth by a lot of small hands.

name: Pair of Clog Irons
desc: Metal soles for clogs, once the sound of every northern street at half past seven in the morning.

name: Whippet Racing Trophy
desc: A small silver cup for a dog that never stopped running, and a man that never stopped saying so.

name: Signed Cricket Ball
desc: Red leather, a faded signature, and a story about who it was that nobody can agree on.

name: Cup Tie Programme
desc: A programme from a muddy cup tie in a January long ago. Team changes in pencil.

name: Velvet Rugby Cap
desc: A tasselled cap, given once per international in the days before the shirts were this big.

name: Child's Hurley
desc: A small ash hurling stick, scuffed from many a back-garden final.

name: Old Elm Dartboard
desc: A dartboard pocked with a thousand small holes. Wire-bound, and the 20 is rather worn.

name: Brewery Ashtray
desc: A heavy glass ashtray with a brewery's name on it, borrowed from a pub in around 1974.

name: Yellowing Telegram
desc: Four words, no stops, and a good deal of feeling: ARRIVING TUESDAY. BOIL KETTLE.

name: Lucky Sixpence
desc: A silver sixpence, once baked into the Christmas pudding. Nobody swallowed it, which is a good sign.

name: Jar of Old Pennies
desc: Big brown pennies from before decimal, in a jam jar. Heavier than they look.

name: Seven-inch Single
desc: A scratched single in a paper sleeve. It skips at the chorus, which is also when it is best.

name: Pocket Transistor Radio
desc: It picks up one station faintly and, on a good night, Luxembourg.

name: Typewriter Key
desc: A single round key marked R, off a machine that typed a thousand letters home.

name: Magic Lantern Slide
desc: A hand-painted glass slide of a sailing ship, to be projected on the parlour wall on a winter night.

name: Aneroid Barometer
desc: Tap the glass and the needle moves. 'Change' is written on it, which is the most honest thing on the dial.

name: Embroidered Sampler
desc: A girl's alphabet in cross-stitch, finished in 1887 and signed, with a little house and a robin.

name: Pressed Flowers
desc: Harebells in a book, brown now, from a walk somebody did not forget.

name: Stick of Rock
desc: A pink stick with a name through the middle, and the name is not yours. Do not eat it.

name: Donkey Bell
desc: A brass bell from a beach donkey who knew exactly how much work he was prepared to do.

name: Roses and Castles Jug
desc: Narrowboat folk art: roses, a castle, and enough painted flowers to make a whole bank holiday.

name: Victorian Tea Caddy
desc: A lockable wooden box for tea, from the days when tea was dear enough to need a key.

name: Sheepdog Whistle
desc: A hand-carved whistle from a shepherd. Dogs hear it for miles. People, mostly, do not.
